identification.title: All Glory Be to Christ
identification.notes: Words by Dustin Kensrue alone, set to the tune of Auld Lang Syne. Integrity Music and PraiseCharts both credit Kensrue as sole author; the Gospel Coalition lists the copyright as Dead Bird Theology and It's All About Jesus Music (ASCAP) and the recording as Kings Kaleidoscope's. Integrity lists CCLI 7008232. The list's guess of Kings Kaleidoscope is right for the recording churches know, but the writer is Kensrue (of Thrice, who also leads worship at his church), not the band. The album and the 2012 year come from the Gospel Coalition post; Integrity's page does not state a year. Reviewed as the song, not any one recording.

claims.structuralNotes: Three verses and a chorus. The first verse sets human achievement and lasting legacy against God's rule and the brevity of life. The chorus calls the congregation to give glory to Christ and acclaim his kingship. The second verse prays for God's will and kingdom and looks to Christ for daily provision and refreshment. The third looks forward to God's faithfulness, the redemptive work of Christ and the renewed creation with God dwelling among his people. The voice is plural, and Christ is named directly. The cross is present as redemption but is not narrated at length.

claims.claim: Human accomplishment and legacy are fleeting, and life is brief; only God endures.
claims.subject: The brevity of life

claims.claim: Glory belongs to Christ, who reigns as king.
claims.subject: The kingship of Christ

claims.claim: The church prays for God's will and kingdom and depends on Christ for daily provision.
claims.subject: Dependence and the kingdom

claims.claim: God is faithful, Christ has accomplished redemption, and creation will be made new with God dwelling among his people.
claims.subject: New creation and redemption

strengths.title: Glory given to Christ as king
strengths.explanation: The chorus gives glory to Christ and acclaims his rule, and the verses place human striving beneath that. A congregation is made to sing who is worthy and who is not.
strengths.scriptureRationale: The Lamb who was slain is worthy of glory - the direction of the chorus's praise.

strengths.title: Mortality set beside the new creation
strengths.explanation: The song is honest about brevity and vanity, then moves to redemption and a renewed creation with God present among his people. Hope is placed in what God does, not in the singer.
strengths.scriptureRationale: He makes all things new - the horizon of the last verse.

strengths.title: A prayer for the kingdom and daily bread
strengths.explanation: The second verse is shaped by the Lord's Prayer, so the congregation prays in Christ's own words while it sings, tying provision to God's will rather than to the singer's effort.
strengths.scriptureRationale: The Lord's Prayer's petitions for the kingdom and for daily bread.

doctrinesAffirmed: The kingship and worthiness of Christ
The brevity of human life and the vanity of achievement
Dependence on God for daily provision
theological.assessment: Nothing to correct. A song that sets human legacy against Christ's reign, prays the Lord's Prayer's petitions, and ends on redemption and new creation. Its weight falls on praise and perspective; the cross is present as redemption without being narrated, so it works best sung beside a text that tells the gospel in full.

strengths.title: A familiar tune with new words
strengths.explanation: Set to Auld Lang Syne, the melody is already in most heads, so a room can sing the chorus on the first pass.

strengths.title: Suits New Year and thanksgiving
strengths.explanation: The theme of fleeting time against God's rule fits a year's end or a service of reflection.

communal.vocalRangeNote: The original recording is in E per Integrity's record; the tune is a familiar folk melody that sits comfortably for most rooms. No chart was read.

range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated.

communal.repetitionAssessment: The chorus returns after each verse and means more each time, since each verse deepens why Christ is worthy of glory.
communal.assessment: Congregational in voice and in tune. The folk-tune setting makes it easy to join and the plural voice keeps the room together. It fits a year's end, a thanksgiving service, or any set that wants a hymn-like sung confession of Christ's kingship.

strengths.title: Christ named outright
strengths.explanation: The chorus names Christ and acclaims him as king, so no one has to guess whom the praise is for.

clarity.assessment: Clear. The Lord's Prayer allusions and the Revelation imagery are familiar to a churchgoer, and the contrast between human legacy and Christ's reign is plain.

synthesis.summary: A congregational song with new words to a familiar tune. It sets the brevity of human achievement against the reign of Christ, gives glory to Christ in the chorus, prays for the kingdom and daily provision, and ends on redemption and the renewed creation. Christ is named. The cross is present as redemption without being narrated. No false claims.

scriptureReferences.relevance: The kingdom and daily bread petitions of the Lord's Prayer - the second verse.
The Lamb is worthy of glory - the direction of the chorus.
God making all things new - the last verse's horizon.
Life as a mist that vanishes - the first verse's observation on brevity.

sources.title: All Glory Be To Christ
sources.establishes: Catalogue record: sole writer Dustin Kensrue, CCLI 7008232, key E, Scripture references Romans, James, Matthew, Revelation, and a summary of what each verse treats.
